newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court will rule on pro-Israeli group.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court will rule on pro-Israeli group.

text.p: The Supreme Court said on Monday it would hear an appeal by the federal election agency of a ruling that could make a pro-Israeli lobbying group subject to campaign law regulations.
The high court agreed to hear a Federal Election Commission appeal of a 1996 lower court ruling that the FEC had misinterpreted the law when it held that the group was not a political organisation.

The FEC decided in 1992 that the group -- the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, known as AIPAC -- was not a political organisation and therefore was not subject to reporting requirements for campaign-related expenditures.
As a political organisation, AIPAC would have to make regular reports to the commission on contributors and limit their contributions to no more than $1,000 per candidate.

A lawsuit challenging the FEC's decision was filed by six individuals including James Akins, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, and Paul Findley, a former Illinois congressman who says AIPAC helped prevent his re-election in 1982.

The Justice Department, in an appeal on behalf of the FEC, which is an independent campaign-finance regulatory agency, urged the Supreme Court to hear the case and overturn the ruling by a federal appeals court.

Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger said the ruling "places substantial burdens on organisations engaged primarily in issue advocacy by requiring that they disclose all of their receipts and disbursements."

He said a group that spends more than $1,000 on contributions or coordinated expenditures a year but is not controlled by a candidate or have nominating or electing candidates as its major purpose is not a political committee.

Dellinger said the ruling wrongly interpreted federal election laws and conflicted with Supreme Court precedent. The Justice Department also argued the individuals who brought the suit did not have the proper legal standing to do so.
The appeals court ruling sent the case back to the FEC for further review of AIPAC's status.
Attorneys for the six individuals, all of whom were formerly diplomats or other government officials, urged the Supreme Court to reject the appeal.

"This is a simple case. AIPAC meets the statutory definition of a 'political committee' because it routinely makes 'contributions' in aggregate amounts likely exceeding $1,000 per year. Nothing more is required," they said.
The Supreme Court will hear arguments in the case and issue a decision in its 1997-98 term, which begins in October.
